title: US plans new tariffs on EU, China and 12 others
summary: The Trump administration is planning new import duties of up to 20% to counter excessive manufacturing abroad. The measures could put further pressure on US consumers already struggling with high…

image.caption: US President Donald Trump speaks at a press conference in February after the Supreme Court struck down his global tariffs [FILE: February 20, 2026]Image: Kevin Lamarque/REUTERS

blocks.text: The Office of the US Trade Representative (USTR) unveiled new tariffs on imports from 14 economies, including the European Union and China.
A senior US official said the proposed duties follow a months-long investigation into allegations that excessive manufacturing abroad puts American producers at a disadvantage.
US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer told CNBC that the proposed tariffs largely stick to rates set under existing trade agreements, although some could be "topped up" by a few percentage points.

China would face an additional tariff of 20%, bringing the combined rate for some Chinese goods to 45%. The proposed duties would respect the 15% tariff cap agreed with the European Union, Japan, South Korea and Taiwan, according to a senior US administration official.
Other affected economies include India, Bangladesh, Cambodia, Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Switzerland, Thailand and Vietnam.
The tariffs could take effect in January at the earliest, following a public comment period.
Why is Trump planning new tariffs?
The measures are also intended to replace revenues lost after the US Supreme Court struck down US president Donald Trump's sweeping global tariffs in February.

The proposed duties could further fuel US inflation, which reached 3.7% in September. High living costs were a key issue in November's midterm elections, in which Trump's Republican Party lost control of both chambers of Congress.
The tariff plans come just weeks before Trump is due to host G20 leaders in Miami in December.
The US official played down concerns about renewed trade tensions and said Washington could sign further trade agreements at the summit.
